title: Caching: what, where, and the cache invalidation problem
story:
There is a well-worn observation that there are only two hard things in computer science, cache invalidation and naming things. It is commonly attributed to Phil Karlton, and worth flagging that the attribution is not firmly documented to an original source — the many numbered variants of the joke are later additions by other people. Which is a small illustration of the thing this curriculum is about: a line everybody can quote, attached to a name almost nobody has checked.

The caching part of it is not a joke, though. Reading is cheap and repeated; computing the answer is expensive and identical every time. So keep the answer somewhere fast and serve the repeats from there. Every system arrives at this independently because the traffic makes it obvious.

Two systems defined how it is done in practice. Memcached, a general-purpose distributed memory caching system, was originally developed by Brad Fitzpatrick for LiveJournal in 2003, and its idea was that a set of web servers could pool their spare memory into one shared lookup layer in front of the database — so capacity came from machines that were already there. Redis, an in-memory data structure store, was first released by Salvatore Sanfilippo in 2009, differing from a plain key-value cache in holding structured values such as lists, sets and sorted sets, and in offering optional persistence. That difference matters more than it sounds: once the cache holds structures rather than opaque blobs, it stops being only a cache and starts being somewhere state lives, which is how so many systems ended up with important data in a component they still describe as a cache.

The difficulty is entirely on the write side, and it is worth being precise about why rather than repeating that invalidation is hard. The moment a cached copy exists there are two representations of one fact, and every write has to decide what happens to both. Update the database first and the cache serves the old value until it is cleared. Clear the cache first and a concurrent read repopulates it from the database before the write lands, so the stale value is restored and now has a fresh expiry. Do both and the second operation can fail on its own, leaving a discrepancy no error message describes. Expire on a timer instead and you have chosen, deliberately or not, how long users see the old answer.

Notice that none of those is a bug to be fixed. They are the available options, and each is a different distribution of the same unavoidable inconsistency. The engineering decision is which one the product can tolerate, which is why this cannot be delegated to a library.

Then there is the failure that arrives at the worst moment. Vattani, Chierichetti and Lowenstein define a cache stampede as what happens when a frequently accessed item expires: multiple requests miss simultaneously and all begin regenerating the same item at once, which severely limits database and web server performance. They note it is often called a cascading failure, because the concurrent recomputations lengthen each individual recomputation by bogging down the system, which in turn pulls even more requests into the stampede.

That self-feeding property is the part to recognise, because it separates this from ordinary overload. The load is being generated by the recovery. The hotter the key, the worse it is — so the item most worth caching is the one whose expiry is most dangerous, which is a genuinely unpleasant property for a mechanism to have.

Their countermeasure is elegant and the shape of it generalises. Let each process randomly request regeneration before the item expires, with the probability rising as expiry approaches. They give algorithms for such probabilistic early expirations which they show to be optimal, and which require no coordination or locks, because every worker decides independently. The randomness is doing the job a lock would do badly: instead of many processes discovering a gap simultaneously, they refresh at staggered moments, and no gap ever opens.

worked.problem: What is a cache stampede, and how do you protect a system when a hot key expires?
worked.reasoning:
A stampede is what happens when a frequently accessed cache item expires: multiple requests miss simultaneously and all begin regenerating the same item at once, which severely limits database and web server performance. It is often called a cascading failure, because the concurrent recomputations lengthen each individual recomputation by bogging down the system, which in turn pulls even more requests into the stampede.

The property worth recognising is in that second sentence. The load is being generated by the recovery, which is what separates this from ordinary overload and which means adding capacity extends the ramp rather than ending it. Each additional recomputation makes every other recomputation slower, which widens the window during which new arrivals also miss.

And the unpleasant structural fact is that the benefit and the failure grow together: the hotter the key, the more worthwhile caching it was, and the more requests arrive in the instant it expires. So the item most worth caching is the one whose expiry is most dangerous, and a cache that has worked perfectly for months gives no warning before its first expiry under real load.

For protection, the published answer is the one I would lead with because it needs no coordination. Let each process randomly request regeneration before the item expires, with the probability of volunteering rising as expiry approaches. Algorithms for such probabilistic early expirations have been shown to be optimal, and they require no locks, because every worker decides independently. The randomness does the job a lock would do badly — rather than many processes discovering a gap at the same moment, they refresh at staggered moments, and no gap ever opens at all. That is the important difference from the alternatives: it prevents the stampede rather than managing one.

The alternatives are worth knowing and worth ranking honestly. A lock so that only one process regenerates while others wait removes the duplicate work but leaves everyone waiting on one recomputation, and introduces a lock in the hot path that can itself fail or be held by a dead process. Refreshing keys in the background before expiry works and requires something outside the request path to know which keys matter, which is a second system to maintain and to keep correct. Serving the stale value while one process refreshes is often the best product answer, because it converts a latency spike into a brief window of old data — but it is only available when old data is acceptable, which is exactly the question the cache raised in the first place.

Which connects back to the general shape of this. The moment a cached copy exists there are two representations of one fact, and every option — every ordering of write and invalidate, every expiry policy, every stampede remedy — is a different distribution of the same unavoidable inconsistency rather than a way of removing it. None of them is a bug being fixed. They are choices about which failure the product can tolerate, which is why this cannot be delegated to a library.

problem.practice: Find your hottest cache key and its expiry policy. Then work out how many requests arrive during one regeneration of it, because that is the number that will hit your database the first time it expires under load.

beats.broke: A database served the same expensive answer repeatedly because nothing remembered it, so traffic that was almost entirely redundant landed on the slowest component in the system.
beats.fix: Keep the computed answer in memory in front of the database, so repeated reads are answered by a lookup rather than by the work that produced the answer.
beats.cost: A second copy of one fact now exists, so every write carries a correctness question — and the copy expiring under load is a failure mode that grows with how valuable the cache was.

interview.q: What is a cache stampede, and how do you protect a system when a hot key expires?
interview.trap: Treating it as ordinary overload and reaching for capacity. The load is generated by the recovery, so more capacity extends the ramp — and each extra concurrent recomputation makes the others slower, widening the window in which new arrivals also miss.
interview.answer:
A stampede is what happens when a frequently accessed item expires: multiple requests miss at once and all begin regenerating the same item, which severely limits database and web server performance. It is often called a cascading failure, because the concurrent recomputations lengthen each individual recomputation by bogging down the system, which pulls even more requests in.

That second sentence is the property to recognise — the load is generated by the recovery, which is what separates it from ordinary overload and why adding capacity extends the ramp rather than ending it.

The structural unpleasantness is that benefit and failure grow together: the hotter the key, the more worthwhile the cache was and the more requests arrive in the instant it expires. So the item most worth caching is the one whose expiry is most dangerous, and a cache that has worked for months gives no warning before its first expiry under real load.

For protection I would lead with the published answer, because it needs no coordination: let each process randomly request regeneration before the item expires, with the probability rising as expiry approaches. Such probabilistic early expirations have been shown optimal and require no locks, since every worker decides independently. The randomness does the job a lock would do badly — processes refresh at staggered moments, so no gap ever opens. That is the key difference: it prevents the stampede rather than managing one.

The alternatives, ranked honestly: a lock so one process regenerates removes duplicate work but leaves everyone waiting on a single recomputation and puts a lock in the hot path that can be held by a dead process. Background refresh before expiry works but needs something outside the request path to know which keys matter — a second system to keep correct. Serving stale while one process refreshes is often the best product answer, converting a latency spike into a brief window of old data, but it is only available when old data is acceptable, which is the question the cache raised in the first place.

All of which is the general shape: once a cached copy exists there are two representations of one fact, and every ordering, expiry policy and remedy is a different distribution of the same unavoidable inconsistency rather than a removal of it.
